Maarten-Jan

looking at your code, I'm wondering why you use the order() function in

x[['Tile']] <- ceiling( 5 * order(o) / length(o));

since o already contains the order of the elements in x. Also note that this implementation of ntile does not have the same behaviour as Oracle's NTILE() function where "The remainder values (the remainder of number of rows divided by buckets) are distributed one for each bucket, starting with bucket 1." (quoted from the Oracle docs <http://docs.oracle.com/cd/B19306_01/server.102/b14200/functions101.htm>)

If you are seeing different behavior between both versions of Renjin, can you provide us with a (fictitious) sample of x such that we can reproduce this issue?

Maarten-Jan

Hi Garvit,

Hard to keep track of all of these moving parts!

Here's what's going on:

(1) The R print() function writes its arguments to the R session's standard output (which probably ends up in your server logs)
(2) The R print() function return its argument x
(3) engine.eval() returns the result of the R expression print(x) which might be org.renjin.sexp.DoubleVector or something similar. The javax.script engine do not print output like a repl console by design.
(4) PrintWriter.println() calls toString() on the result of engine.eval() and send this string to the servlet's response. This is where you're getting the debugging string.

You might look at other R functions that format your object to a string (or generate html tables for example), but if you just want the interactive output, you can provide an alternate standard out for the renjin session which you can capture and send as a response.

Best,
Alex

For S3 generics, selection of overloads is done by name. For example, if your new class is "blue" and you want to provide a generic for the unique() function, you can declare a function such as:

unique.blue <- function(my.blue.object) {
  # your class-specific implementation
}

You could then eventually call into a java method within that R function.

You could also bind (assign) a static Java method directly to the right name, for example,

unique.blue <- MyBlueUtils$unique

hth,
Alex

To come back to the R SPARQL package:

I find the approach used by the rrdf package more interesting from Renjin's perspective. rrdf, and more specifically the rrdflib package, uses rJava to use the Apache Jena RDF API and SPARQL engine. The author of those packages, Egon Willighagen, has recently written an open-access paper on these (https://peerj.com/preprints/185/) and which contains examples on rrdf's usage.

As Renjin is a Java application, it makes sense to follow the same approach. That is, to create an rrdf package for Renjin which uses the Apache Jena library.

Just my 2 cents...

Maarten-Jan
